If $\epsilon $ is sufficiently small and $\M $ satisfies the $\Phi $-pinching and $r$-canonical neighborhood assumptions, then for every $A<\infty $ and $\widehat r>0$ there are $\xi =\xi (A)>0$ and $K=K(A,\widehat r)<\infty $ such that, whenever $Q=R(x_0,t_0)>0$, $\Phi (Q)/Q<\xi $, and $\dist _{t_0}(x_0,x)\leq A Q^{-1/2}$, one has $R(x,t_0)\leq KQ$, with $K=K(A,r(t_0))$.
Proof

Canonical neighborhoods force the blowup points into strong $\epsilon $-necks, where the strong maximum principle contradicts the cone limit.

\label{claim2II.4.2}
If $\epsilon$ is sufficiently small and $\M$ satisfies the $\Phi$-pinching
and $r$-canonical neighborhood assumptions, then for every $A<\infty$ and
$\widehat r>0$ there are $\xi=\xi(A)>0$ and $K=K(A,\widehat r)<\infty$ such
that, whenever $Q=R(x_0,t_0)>0$, $\Phi(Q)/Q<\xi$, and
$\dist_{t_0}(x_0,x)\leq A Q^{-1/2}$, one has
$R(x,t_0)\leq KQ$, with $K=K(A,r(t_0))$.
\end{lemma}
